cards.p: Bitcoin was created in 2009 as money that no bank or government controls. Instead of one bank keeping the ledger of who owns what, thousands of computers around the world keep identical copies of it - that shared ledger is called a blockchain.

Stock markets open and close. Crypto trades 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, everywhere on Earth at once. Prices can move violently at 3 AM on a Sunday - which is exactly why traders use alerts and stop-losses instead of watching charts all day.

cards.h: Thousands of coins, a few that matter
cards.p: Bitcoin (BTC) is the largest and moves the whole market. Ethereum (ETH) is second. Beyond the top handful, thousands of smaller coins (altcoins) exist - most are far riskier and less liquid. As a beginner, everything you need to learn can be learned on BTC and ETH.

quiz.q: What keeps track of who owns which crypto?
o: A shared ledger copied across thousands of computers (blockchain)
Each exchange keeps its own private list, with no shared record

quiz.q: When does the crypto market close?
As a beginner, which coins are the sensible place to learn?
o: BTC and ETH - the largest and most liquid
Whatever is trending on social media

lessons.t: Exchanges, wallets and what buying means

cards.p: An exchange is a marketplace that matches buyers and sellers - Binance, Coinbase, Kraken and Bybit are exchanges. When you buy Bitcoin there, the exchange updates its internal ledger; the coins sit in the exchange custody until you withdraw them.

Buying the actual coin is called spot trading - you own it, and your maximum loss is what you paid. Derivatives (like the futures you will meet in Course 2) are contracts that track the price without owning the coin - they allow leverage, which cuts both ways.

cards.h: Not your keys, not your coins
cards.p: A wallet is where crypto lives when it is truly yours - controlled by a secret key only you hold. Coins left on an exchange are an IOU from that exchange. That is fine for active trading amounts, but history (Mt. Gox, FTX) shows why large holdings belong in your own wallet.

quiz.q: What is spot trading?
o: Betting on price with borrowed money
Buying the actual coin - you own it

quiz.q: Coins sitting on an exchange are…
o: Always perfectly safe no matter what happens to the exchange
Effectively an IOU from the exchange

quiz.q: What is the maximum you can lose buying spot with $100?

cards.p: Each candle summarises price over a period: where it opened, closed, and the highest and lowest points touched. A green candle closed higher than it opened; a red one closed lower. The thin lines (wicks) show the extremes price briefly touched.

act.prompt: Tap the UPPER WICK of the candle - the line showing the highest price touched.

cards.p: Before moving on, prove it to your eyes. One tap.

The same market looks different on different timeframes. A 1-minute chart shows noise; a daily chart shows the trend. A common beginner mistake is panicking over a scary 5-minute candle that is invisible on the daily chart. Zoom out first, always.

Volume shows how much was actually traded. A price move on high volume means real participation; the same move on thin volume is fragile and often reverses. Price tells you what happened - volume tells you how much to believe it.

quiz.q: A red candle means…
o: Price closed lower than it opened
Price is guaranteed to keep falling for the rest of the day

quiz.q: What do the candle wicks show?
o: The price the market predicts for the next period
The highest and lowest prices touched in that period

quiz.q: A big price move on very low volume is…
o: Always the start of a trend

lessons.t: Market cap, liquidity and why price alone lies

cards.h: Price per coin means nothing by itself
cards.p: A coin costing $0.001 is not cheaper than Bitcoin in any meaningful way. What matters is market cap: price × circulating supply. A $0.001 coin with 100 billion tokens is a $100M project. It only needs to reach $1 is the oldest trap in crypto.

cards.h: Liquidity: can you actually get out?
cards.p: Liquidity is how much you can buy or sell without moving the price. BTC absorbs millions of dollars per second; a small altcoin might crash 10% from a single large sell. Illiquid coins are easy to enter and brutal to exit - exactly when you most need to.

When you buy at market, you pay whatever sellers are asking right now. In a thin market, your own order pushes the price - the difference between the price you saw and the price you got is slippage. It is a real cost, and it grows with position size and shrinks with liquidity.

quiz.q: What determines a coin's real size?
o: How high it ranks and how often it is mentioned on social media

quiz.q: Liquidity measures…
o: How fast the blockchain confirms new transactions
How much you can trade without moving the price
The number of coins in supply

quiz.q: Slippage is…
o: A fixed trading fee that the exchange sets in advance for every order
The gap between the price you saw and the price your market order filled at

cards.h: A small boat on a big ocean
cards.p: Crypto's total market is tiny compared with stocks or bonds, and much of it trades with leverage. The same wave of money that barely moves the S&P 500 can move Bitcoin several percent - and smaller coins several times more.

Big moves usually combine three things: a trigger (news, a macro number), thin liquidity (nights, weekends), and forced selling from leveraged traders being liquidated. That third ingredient - which you will study in Course 2 - is why crypto crashes are so fast and so deep.

Volatility is not a bug - it is why traders are here. But it is symmetric: the same 10% move that doubles a leveraged account also erases one. Every lesson after this one is really about surviving volatility long enough to benefit from it.

quiz.q: Why does the same amount of money move crypto more than stocks?
o: Crypto prices are manipulated by exchanges whenever volume is low
The crypto market is much smaller and more leveraged

quiz.q: Which ingredient makes crypto crashes especially fast and deep?
o: Forced selling from liquidated leveraged traders
Sudden increases in mining difficulty across the network

quiz.q: Volatility for a trader is…
o: Pure risk to be avoided entirely

cards.p: A stablecoin is a crypto token designed to stay worth exactly $1 - USDT and USDC are the giants. They exist so traders can hold dollars inside crypto: park profits, escape volatility, and price everything else against a stable unit.

Every market is a PAIR: the thing you trade and the thing you price it in. BTC/USDT means Bitcoin priced in Tether dollars. When you sell BTC in that pair you receive USDT, not bank dollars. Nearly all futures you will trade are USDT-margined pairs.

A stablecoin is only as good as what backs it. Depegs have happened - most famously Terra UST collapsing to zero in 2022. For trading balances the big issuers have held up, but know what you hold: a token redeemable for dollars, not dollars themselves.

quiz.q: What is a stablecoin designed to do?
o: Grow by a steady 10% every single year

quiz.q: In the pair BTC/USDT, what do you receive when you sell BTC?
Stablecoins are…

lessons.t: Fees: the silent tax on every trade

cards.p: Every trade pays. The taker fee (crossing the spread instantly, market orders) is higher; the maker fee (resting limit orders that add liquidity) is lower - sometimes even a rebate. The spread itself - the gap between best bid and ask - is a cost too.

Futures fees are charged on the NOTIONAL, not your margin. At 20x leverage, a 0.055% taker fee is 1.1% of your margin per side - over 2% round-trip. Ten trades a day at that rate is a fee bill few strategies can outrun.

Most losing beginners do not lose to bad direction - they bleed out on fees and spread from trading too often. Fewer, better trades with limit entries is not just discipline advice; it is arithmetic. Count your fees weekly in your journal and treat them as a position against you.

quiz.q: Which order type usually pays the LOWER fee?
Futures fees are charged on…
o: Only the margin you posted for the trade

quiz.q: At 20x leverage a 0.055% taker fee costs roughly what share of your margin per side?

cards.p: Crypto has moved in dramatic cycles: accumulation (quiet, nobody cares), markup (the bull run everyone joins late), distribution (smart money sells into euphoria) and markdown (the bear that convinces everyone it is over). Every cycle feels unprecedented; the emotions are identical.

Each cycle crowns new stories - ICOs, DeFi, NFTs, AI coins. The story changes; the pattern does not: a real innovation, a speculative frenzy far beyond it, a collapse that kills the weak projects, and a base for the next cycle built from the survivors.

You cannot time cycles precisely, but you can locate yourself roughly: is greed extreme, is your barber recommending coins, are 100x memecoins outperforming everything? Late-cycle conditions are when reducing risk matters most - exactly when it feels least necessary.

quiz.q: In which phase does smart money typically SELL?
o: Accumulation, while nobody is paying attention yet

quiz.q: What repeats across every crypto cycle?
o: The emotional pattern: disbelief, euphoria, despair
The same narratives return and lead every single cycle

quiz.q: When does reducing risk matter most?

cards.h: If it promises returns, it is the product
cards.p: Guaranteed 2% a day. A trading bot with no losing months. A stranger offering to manage your funds. Every one of these is a scam, always, without exception - real trading has losing periods, and nobody with a printing press shares it with strangers.

cards.h: The classics: rug pulls and phishing
cards.p: A rug pull is a token whose creators drain the liquidity once buyers pile in - endemic among fresh micro-caps. Phishing is a fake exchange or wallet site harvesting your login or seed phrase. Bookmark real sites; never click login links from messages.

cards.h: Basic hygiene that stops 95% of it
cards.p: Use 2FA (an authenticator app, not SMS) on every exchange. Never share a seed phrase with anyone, ever - no support agent needs it. Be paranoid about direct messages: real platforms do not DM you first. Boring rules, and they are the whole game.

quiz.q: A service guarantees 2% daily returns. It is…
Who legitimately needs your seed phrase?
The best 2FA method is…
o: SMS codes sent to your registered phone number

courses.name: Candlestick Patterns
courses.sub: Reading the battle, candle by candle

cards.p: A doji is a candle that closes almost exactly where it opened - a long fight between buyers and sellers that ended in a draw. Alone it means indecision. Its POSITION gives it meaning: a doji after a long trend says the winning side is running out of conviction.

A doji in the middle of a range is noise - indecision inside indecision. A doji at a key resistance after five green candles is a real signal: the buyers who pushed price up just failed to push further. Same candle, completely different message.

A doji is a question mark, not an answer. It asks: is the trend tired? The answer comes from the NEXT candle and the level it happens at. Doji at resistance + red confirmation candle = a story. Doji alone = a coin flip with a fancy name.

quiz.q: A doji tells you…
o: Buyers won the session decisively and remain in control
The session ended in a draw - indecision

quiz.q: Where does a doji actually MATTER?
o: In the middle of a range, where both sides keep hesitating
After a long trend at a key level

quiz.q: The right way to act on a doji is…
o: Enter immediately, before the opportunity disappears
Wait for the next candle to confirm at the level

cards.p: A bullish engulfing pattern is a red candle followed by a green one whose body completely swallows it. Everyone who sold during that red candle is now underwater - and the message is blunt: buyers just took control at this price.

It is trapped-trader mechanics, not magic. The sellers from the engulfed candle have losing positions; their exits (buy-backs) add fuel to the new direction. The bigger the engulfed candle and the more important the level, the more trapped traders - and the stronger the signal.

cards.h: The checklist for a real engulf
cards.p: Three requirements: it happens AT a level (support for bullish, resistance for bearish), the engulfing body fully covers the previous body, and volume rises on the engulfing candle. Missing all three? You are looking at two random candles.

quiz.q: A bullish engulfing is…
o: Two green candles of equal size closing at the same level
A green body that completely swallows the previous red body

quiz.q: The mechanical reason engulfing patterns work is…
o: Trapped traders from the engulfed candle fuel the reversal as they exit
Exchanges promoting the coin to attract fresh buyers into the move

quiz.q: A real engulf needs…
o: Level + full body coverage + rising volume
Confirmation from several large accounts on social media

lessons.t: Hammer and shooting star: the rejection wicks

cards.p: A hammer appears after a decline: a small body at the top with a long lower wick - at least twice the body. The story: sellers pushed price far down during the session, and buyers slammed it all the way back. That long wick is a failed breakdown, written in one candle.

act.prompt: One of these three candles is a hammer. Tap it.

cards.p: Remember: small body on top, long lower wick, after a decline.

cards.h: The shooting star - the same story, upside down
cards.p: A shooting star is the mirror image at the top of a rally: long UPPER wick, small body at the bottom. Buyers tried to continue the rally, got rejected hard, and the candle closed near its low. At resistance, it is one of the cleanest short setups candles can print.

quiz.q: A hammer's long lower wick shows…
o: Sellers pushed down and buyers rejected the entire move
A trading halt triggered by the exchange during the session

quiz.q: A hammer matters most…
A shooting star is…
o: A hammer that appears at the bottom of a long decline
A long upper wick rejection at the top of a rally

cards.p: The morning star is a three-act reversal at the bottom: a strong red candle (sellers in control), a tiny-bodied candle (the fight stalls - often a doji), then a strong green candle closing deep into the first one (buyers take over). The evening star is the same pattern flipped, at the top.

A single candle can be noise; three consecutive candles telling one coherent story is harder to fake. The middle candle is the hinge - the moment momentum died. The third candle is the proof. Without the strong third close, you have a stall, not a reversal.

Stronger when: the middle candle gaps or stands clearly apart, the third candle closes past the midpoint of the first, and the whole pattern sits at a level from your map. As always - the pattern gives the trigger and the invalidation (beyond the star's extreme), the level gives the reason.

quiz.q: The morning star's middle candle represents…
o: A sudden acceleration of the existing trend direction
The moment momentum stalls - the hinge

quiz.q: The reversal is confirmed by…
o: The middle candle alone, without any further movement
A strong third candle closing deep into the first

quiz.q: The stop for a star pattern belongs…
o: Always exactly 1% away from the entry price

cards.p: An inside bar sits entirely within the range of the previous candle - lower high, higher low. The market is compressing: ranges shrink, both sides wait. You already know from m7 what compression promises: expansion. A cluster of inside bars is a spring being wound.

The classic setup: mark the mother bar's high and low. A break of one side with volume is the trigger; the opposite side is the natural invalidation. It is one of the tightest risk-to-reward structures in trading, because the stop distance is the coil's width.

Compression breaks FAIL often - the first move is frequently the fake (you know this from a2's spring). Protect against it: prefer breaks in the higher-timeframe trend direction, demand volume, and never chase a break that instantly returns inside the mother bar - that reentry IS the failure signal.

quiz.q: An inside bar is…
o: A candle noticeably bigger than the previous candle
A candle entirely within the previous candle's range

quiz.q: The natural stop for an inside-bar breakout is…
o: The opposite side of the mother bar
A fixed 10% away from the breakout price

quiz.q: A break that instantly returns inside the mother bar is…
o: A confirmation that the breakout is genuine and safe to chase
The failure signal - do not chase it

cards.p: Wicks are rejected prices - and their location tells you who is being rejected. Repeated long lower wicks at one zone mean someone is absorbing the selling there: every dip gets bought. Repeated upper wicks at a zone mean supply sits above and every rally gets sold.

A HUGE wick after an extended move - much larger than recent candles - often marks exhaustion: the final burst of the trend met a wall of opposite orders (this is the liquidation-cascade wick from m5 seen up close). Trend + climax volume + giant wick = the move is likely done for now.

cards.h: Wick clusters draw your levels for you
cards.p: Forget drawing lines by feel: zones where multiple wicks poke and reject ARE the market's own support and resistance. Draw the zone across the wick tips, then apply the full toolkit - trend, volume node, positioning - at that zone.

quiz.q: Repeated long lower wicks at one zone suggest…
o: Someone is absorbing the selling - dips get bought
Sellers are winning and will keep pressing the zone lower

quiz.q: A giant wick after an extended trend often marks…
o: Continuation of the trend with even more strength behind it
Exhaustion - the climax met a wall of orders

quiz.q: The best support/resistance zones are drawn from…
o: Round numbers only, because everyone watches them anyway

cards.h: Every pattern has a failure rate
cards.p: Hammers get run over. Engulfs get engulfed. In crypto's stop-hunting environment (a1), textbook patterns fail CONSTANTLY - because everyone sees them, and visible orders are food. Accepting this is the difference between a pattern user and a pattern victim.

cards.h: The failed pattern IS a pattern
cards.p: Here is the professional secret: a FAILED signal is often a better signal. A bullish hammer at support that breaks down means every hammer-buyer is now trapped - their stops fuel the move down. Trading the failure (with the trapped crowd as fuel) is often cleaner than trading the textbook.

Practical rule: know in advance what invalidates the pattern, and what the failure trade would look like. If the hammer low breaks, do you exit only - or flip? Deciding this before entry turns a pattern from a prayer into a plan with two branches.

quiz.q: Textbook patterns in crypto fail often because…
A failed bullish pattern often becomes…
o: A strong bearish signal - trapped buyers fuel the move
An even stronger buy signal for patient bulls

quiz.q: Before entering a pattern trade you should know…
o: Only the profit target, since the pattern confirms the direction
What invalidates it and what the failure trade looks like

cards.p: A candle pattern is a TRIGGER, never a reason. The reason comes from everything else you have learned: trend (m1), level (m1/a4), positioning (m4), regime (a7). The candle only answers the final question: is NOW the moment to act at this level?

Top-down: daily trend allows the direction → 4H shows a setup at a level → positioning is not crowded against you → THEN you zoom in and wait for the candle - the engulf, the hammer, the star - as your entry trigger with a built-in invalidation. Candles without that stack are gambling with extra steps.

cards.h: Train the eye, then trust the process
cards.p: Pattern recognition is a skill that builds with reps - and paper trading gives you unlimited reps for free. Spot a pattern, write the two-branch plan, execute, journal it. A hundred logged patterns later, you will KNOW which ones pay you - in your market, on your timeframe.

quiz.q: In a complete trade, a candle pattern is…
The correct sequence ends with the candle because…
o: Candles predict everything that happens on the higher timeframes
It times the entry at a level that already had reasons

quiz.q: The way to learn which patterns pay YOU is…
o: A hundred logged reps in paper trading + the journal
Memorizing the names and shapes of every known pattern

try.p: Go pattern hunting: open a chart, find one engulf or hammer at a real level, and log the two-branch plan as a paper trade.

cards.p: A futures contract is an agreement that tracks a coin's price. You never own the Bitcoin - you hold a position that gains or loses exactly as the price moves. Crypto's favourite version is the perpetual future (perp), which has no expiry date: you can hold it as long as your margin survives.

With futures you can profit in both directions: going long means you gain when price rises; going short means you gain when price falls. Tap the buttons below and watch the same price move flip from profit to loss.

Perpetual futures are the most traded product in crypto - daily perp volume dwarfs spot. They are popular for exactly the two features that make them dangerous: leverage, and the ability to short. Everything in this course exists because of what you will learn in the next two lessons.

quiz.q: When you buy a perpetual future, you own…
o: A position that tracks the price - no coins
A small ownership share of the exchange itself

quiz.q: A short position profits when…
What makes a perpetual future perpetual?

cards.p: Leverage lets you control a position bigger than your money. Put down $100 of margin at 10× leverage and you control a $1,000 position. Every 1% the price moves, your position gains or loses $10 - which is 10% of YOUR money. The multiplier applies to losses exactly as it does to gains.

act.prompt: Drag the slider until a routine 1% move against you would wipe 100% of your margin.

cards.p: The red marker is your liquidation. Watch what leverage does to it.

At 100× leverage, a 1% move against you wipes 100% of your margin. Bitcoin moves 1% routinely - several times a day. That is not a market crash; it is background noise. High leverage does not make a strategy better, it just compresses the time until a normal wiggle takes you out.

quiz.q: You open $100 at 10× leverage. Price moves 1% in your favour. Your profit is about…
The notional of a $100 position at 20× is…
At 100× leverage, what price move against you erases your whole margin?

try.p: Open the position size calculator and see how notional and risk change as you slide leverage from 5× to 100×.
try.label: Position Size Calculator →

lessons.t: Liquidation: the point of no return

cards.p: When a leveraged position loses almost all its margin, the exchange force-closes it to protect itself - that is liquidation. Your position is gone, your margin is gone, and no recovery is possible even if price bounces one second later. It is the single most important price on your screen.

act.prompt: Now do the opposite: drag the leverage DOWN until your liquidation sits at least 10% away from entry.

cards.p: This is the exact decision you will make on every real trade.

cards.h: Why it will bounce back does not apply
cards.p: A spot holder can ride a 30% dip and wait years. A liquidated futures trader cannot - the position no longer exists. This asymmetry is THE difference between spot and leverage: spot punishes patience-free traders slowly, leverage executes them instantly.

quiz.q: After liquidation, if the price immediately recovers, you…
o: Get your position back automatically at the same price
Get nothing - the position is gone

quiz.q: At roughly what adverse move does a 50× position liquidate?
The first thing to know before opening any leveraged trade is…

try.p: Compute a real liquidation price: entry, leverage, side - see exactly where the position dies.
try.label: Liquidation Calculator →

lessons.t: Longs, shorts and how P&L actually works

cards.h: The P&L formula in plain words
cards.p: Your profit or loss = position size × the percentage the price moved. ROE - return on equity - is that P&L measured against your margin. Drag the price move below and watch both numbers react at 10× leverage on a $100 margin.

cards.h: Shorting is not evil, it is a tool
cards.p: Shorting - profiting from falls - feels unnatural at first. But markets fall faster than they rise (down the elevator, up the stairs), and a trader who can only long is blind in half the market. In a paper account, practise both until neither feels special.

Every open and close pays a fee on the notional, and perpetuals exchange periodic funding payments between longs and shorts (next lesson). At high leverage these small costs compound into a meaningful headwind - another quiet reason overtraders lose.

quiz.q: You are long $1,000 notional and price rises 3%. Your P&L is…
Down the elevator, up the stairs means…
o: Markets fall faster than they rise
Markets rise faster than they fall

quiz.q: Trading fees on futures are charged on…

cards.h: How perps stay glued to the real price
cards.p: With no expiry, a perpetual could drift away from the actual coin price. Funding prevents that: every few hours, one side pays the other a small percentage. Toggle below: when perps trade ABOVE spot (crowd is long), longs pay shorts; BELOW spot, shorts pay longs.

Extreme positive funding means the crowd is heavily long AND paying for the privilege - historically a warning sign, because crowded trades unwind violently. Extreme negative funding marks crowded shorts, fuel for a short squeeze.

Funding of 0.01% per 8 hours sounds like nothing - but that is about 11% per year on your notional, and at 10× leverage it is a triple-digit annualised drag on margin. Position holders who ignore funding find their P&L quietly leaking.

quiz.q: When the perp trades above the spot price, who pays funding?
Extremely positive funding usually signals…
o: A heavily crowded long side - squeeze risk
A long stretch of low volatility ahead for the market

quiz.q: Why does small funding matter at high leverage?
o: It compounds into a large annualised drag on your margin
It is always refunded when you close the position

cards.p: A market order fills instantly at whatever the book offers - you pay the spread and any slippage. A limit order names your price and waits. A stop order triggers when price crosses a level. The picture below shows all three living on the order book.

cards.h: Market: speed for a price. Limit: price for patience.
cards.p: Use market orders when getting in or out RIGHT NOW matters more than the exact price - knowing slippage is worst during violent moves. Professional entries are mostly limits: you may never get filled, but when you do it is at your price or better, usually with lower fees.

The stop order is the foundation of the stop-loss (Course 3). It executes your plan when you are asleep, at work, or emotionally compromised. The trader who watches the chart instead is the trader who freezes at the worst moment.

quiz.q: The guaranteed-fill, price-uncertain order is…
A limit order guarantees…
The main purpose of a stop order is…
o: Getting a better entry price than the current market offers
Executing your exit plan automatically when a level breaks

cards.h: Two ways to back a position
cards.p: Isolated margin walls off a fixed amount for one position - if it liquidates, you lose only that wall. Cross margin lets your ENTIRE futures balance back every position - more room before liquidation, but a blowup can take the whole account with it.

Isolated is the beginner default and the honest choice for risky trades: the damage is predefined. Cross suits hedged books and experienced traders who actively manage margin. Using cross to survive a bad trade longer is not a strategy - it is a bigger funeral.

Exchanges default differently, and the margin mode changes your liquidation price dramatically. It is part of the pre-trade ritual: side, size, leverage, margin mode, liquidation price. Every time, no exceptions.

quiz.q: In isolated margin, a liquidation costs you…
o: Your whole account balance, including every open position
Only the margin walled off for that position

quiz.q: Cross margin means…
o: Only one position is allowed to be open at any time
Your entire balance backs every position

quiz.q: Using cross margin to delay a losing trade is…

cards.h: Two prices on the same screen
cards.p: Last price is the most recent trade on YOUR exchange. Mark price is a fair-value blend of several exchanges plus the spot index. They differ by pennies in calm markets - and meaningfully in violent ones or on thin venues.

Exchanges liquidate on MARK, not last. This protects you: a single manipulated wick on one venue cannot liquidate positions everywhere. It also explains the classic confusion - you can be liquidated when the chart wick on your screen never touched your level, because mark got there.

Trade decisions: last price (that is where your orders fill). Survival math: mark price (that is what liquidation and unrealized P&L use). Serious platforms show both - learn where yours displays mark, and set alarms on it, not on the candle wick.

quiz.q: Liquidations are triggered by…
o: Last traded price on your exchange
Mark price - a multi-exchange fair value

quiz.q: Why do exchanges use mark price for liquidations?
o: One venue's manipulated wick cannot liquidate everyone
Financial regulators require it on every licensed venue

quiz.q: Your position was liquidated but the chart wick never touched your liq level. Most likely…
o: The exchange took the position on purpose to collect the margin
Mark price reached the level even though last price did not

lessons.t: Maintenance margin: the real liq math

cards.h: Why liq is not exactly 100 ÷ leverage
cards.p: The exchange requires a safety buffer - maintenance margin (often around 0.5% of notional) - kept aside at all times. Liquidation fires when your equity falls TO that buffer, not to zero. So a 10x long liquidates around −9.5%, not exactly −10%.

Maintenance margin is tiered: enormous positions require a higher percentage, because force-closing them moves the market. This is one reason whale liquidation levels sit closer to entry than the simple formula suggests.

On large positions many exchanges liquidate in slices - closing part of the position to bring margin back above maintenance, rather than nuking it all at once. Helpful, but do not rely on it: by the time partial liquidation is saving you, the trade has already failed.

quiz.q: A 10x long liquidates at roughly…
o: Exactly −10%, as the simple leverage formula suggests

quiz.q: Maintenance margin is…
o: A one-time fee charged when the position is opened
A safety buffer the exchange requires at all times

quiz.q: Partial liquidation means…
o: You immediately lose half of your entire account balance
The exchange closes slices of a big position to restore margin

cards.h: The trade begins after the entry
cards.p: Beginners obsess over entries; professionals manage what happens next. A live position is a series of decisions: is the thesis still valid, has the invalidation moved, is the size still right? Managing is not fiddling - it is executing the plan you wrote before entry.

Closing part of a winner at the first target banks real profit while the rest rides. It converts a paper win into a certain one, calms the mind, and keeps you in the trend. The classic structure: take a portion at 1R, move the stop, let the remainder work.

cards.h: Breakeven stops: free trades, used carefully
cards.p: After price moves meaningfully in your favour, moving the stop to entry makes the trade risk-free - psychologically priceless. Do it too early and normal noise stops you out of a good trade. Give it room: breakeven AFTER the first target, not the first green minute.

quiz.q: A partial close at the first target…
o: Banks certain profit while the rest rides
Only doubles your trading fees without any real benefit

quiz.q: Moving your stop to breakeven makes the trade…
o: Risk-free (excluding gaps) - but do it too early and noise stops you out
Guaranteed to end profitable no matter what happens next

quiz.q: The right time to manage a position is…
o: According to the plan written BEFORE entry
Whenever the position starts to feel scary or exciting

cards.p: Profit comes from position SIZE times price move. Leverage only decides how much margin you post for that size. A $1,000 position makes the same $30 on a 3% move whether it uses 2x or 50x - the 50x version just liquidates 25 times sooner.

Professional desks routinely run single-digit effective leverage. The 100x button exists because it is profitable for exchanges, not for users. High leverage is a liquidity-efficiency tool for hedgers and scalpers measured in seconds - not a wealth machine.

Leverage lets you keep less capital on a (hackable, freezable) exchange for the same exposure - that is capital efficiency. Used with tiny position sizes it is legitimate. Used to maximise size it converts normal volatility into certain ruin, on a timer.

quiz.q: Two traders hold the same $1,000 position; one at 2x, one at 50x. A 3% favourable move pays…
The 100x option exists mainly because…
o: Professional traders demand it for their strategies

quiz.q: The legitimate benefit of leverage is…
o: Bigger guaranteed profits on every single winning trade
Keeping less capital on-exchange for the same exposure

cards.p: A position ticket shows: side and leverage (LONG 10x), entry price, mark price, size or notional, margin, liquidation price, unrealized P&L and ROE. You now know every one of these. If any number on a live ticket confuses you, do not add size - decode it first.

cards.h: The two numbers that matter most
cards.p: Liquidation price (how far is death?) and position size (how much do I lose per 1% move?). P&L and ROE are outputs - they follow from the two inputs. Traders who watch only the green/red number manage feelings; traders who watch liq distance and size manage risk.

Open a paper position and read the whole ticket out loud: side, leverage, entry, size, margin, liquidation and its distance, stop, target. When that takes you ten seconds and zero confusion, Course 2 has done its job.

quiz.q: The two most important numbers on a live ticket are…
o: The live P&L and ROE numbers at the top of the ticket

quiz.q: ROE on a ticket measures P&L against…
If a number on your ticket confuses you, you should…
o: Decode it before touching the position
Ask about it in the chat and keep trading meanwhile

courses.name: Risk Management
courses.sub: The only edge beginners can actually have

cards.h: Risk a slice, never the pie

act.prompt: Drag your risk-per-trade down until you could survive at least 30 losses in a row.

cards.p: Professionals size positions so one losing trade costs a fixed small share of the account - commonly 1-2%. Watch what your risk setting does to survival.

cards.h: Size from the stop, not from greed
cards.p: The correct order: choose where the trade is wrong (your stop-loss level), measure the distance from entry to stop, then size the position so that distance equals your 1-2% risk. Size is an OUTPUT of the calculation - never the starting point.

cards.h: Leverage is a tool, size is the decision
cards.p: Leverage only determines how much margin you post for a given size; the risk comes from the size itself. A properly-sized 10× trade risks less than an oversized 2× trade. Stop asking what leverage should I use and start asking what size keeps my risk at 1%.

quiz.q: With 1% risk per trade, how many straight losses leave you 80% intact?
What is the correct FIRST step of sizing a trade?
o: Deciding where the trade is wrong (the stop level)
Maximising the position size your margin allows

quiz.q: Risk ultimately comes from…
o: The leverage multiplier alone, nothing else
Position size relative to your stop distance

try.p: Size a real trade: account, risk %, entry and stop - the calculator returns the exact position size.

lessons.t: Stop-loss and take-profit, placed like a pro

cards.h: The stop goes where the idea dies
cards.p: A stop-loss belongs at the price where your trade thesis is proven wrong - below the support you bought, beyond the level that invalidates the setup. Placing it at the most pain I can tolerate is backwards: the market does not know or care about your pain threshold.

act.prompt: You bought at the green line because of the support zone. Tap where the stop-loss belongs.

cards.p: One of these three spots is right. Two of them are how beginners lose.

cards.h: Stop-hunting is real, panic about it is not
cards.p: Price often wicks through obvious levels, triggers clustered stops, then reverses. The fix is not removing your stop (that converts a small loss into a liquidation) - it is placing stops beyond obvious round numbers and sizing so a stop-out is boring, not devastating.

cards.h: Take-profit: decide while you are sane
cards.p: A take-profit order banks the win automatically. Decide the exit before entering, while you are objective - because after entry you become the least objective person watching that chart. Partial take-profits (closing, say, half at the first target) are a legitimate compromise.

quiz.q: The best place for a stop-loss is…
o: Where losing would hurt too much
Where the trade idea is proven wrong
As close to entry as possible

quiz.q: When price hunts stops through an obvious level, the right response is…
o: Never use stop-loss orders again on any trade
Place stops beyond obvious levels and size so a stop-out is tolerable

quiz.q: When should the exit plan be decided?
o: After the trade is in profit

try.p: Open a paper position and attach a real SL and TP to it - practise the full ritual with zero risk.
try.label: Paper Trade →

cards.p: Risk:reward compares what you risk with what you aim to win. Risking $50 to make $150 is 1:3. At 1:3, winning just 3 trades out of 10 leaves you profitable - the picture below is those ten trades. The ratio buys you the right to be wrong most of the time.

cards.h: Win rate and R:R trade off
cards.p: High win-rate strategies usually have small wins; high R:R strategies lose often but win big. Both work; neither works with a bad combination (low win rate AND low R:R - the default state of an impulsive beginner). Know which game your strategy plays.

cards.h: Expectancy: the only number that decides
cards.p: Expectancy = (win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss). Positive means the approach makes money over many trades; negative means no position sizing can save it. One trade means nothing - expectancy is measured across dozens.

quiz.q: At 1:3 risk:reward, what win rate is roughly break-even?
A strategy with negative expectancy…
o: Works fine as long as you trade a smaller size
Loses money over time no matter the sizing

quiz.q: How many trades does it take to judge a strategy?
o: It cannot be measured with any real accuracy

try.p: Feed your win rate and R:R into the Risk of Ruin calculator - see what the math says about your survival odds.
try.label: Risk of Ruin Calculator →

act.prompt: Drag the loss deeper and watch what recovery requires. Find the loss where you need +100% just to get back.

cards.p: Lose 10% and you need 11% to recover. This asymmetry is not motivational-poster material - it is arithmetic, and it is the reason capital preservation beats profit-chasing.

cards.h: Streaks are normal, ruin is optional
cards.p: Even a strategy that wins 60% of the time will hit 5-loss streaks regularly - that is probability, not failure. Whether a normal streak becomes account-ending depends entirely on the size you risked per trade. Sizing turns variance into noise; oversizing turns it into ruin.

After a loss, the urge is to size UP to win it back fast. That is exactly backwards: bigger size after losses means your worst decisions get your largest bets. Professionals do the opposite - size down in drawdowns, back up when performing.

quiz.q: After losing 50% of an account, recovery requires…
A 5-loss streak on a good strategy is…
After a losing streak, professionals typically…

lessons.t: Psychology: the enemy in the mirror

cards.p: The most expensive trade in any beginner's history is the one placed 90 seconds after a painful loss - oversized, unplanned, driven by the need to be made whole. Name the pattern now, and adopt the professional rule: after a stop-out, no new trade until a written plan exists.

A coin already up 30% today feels safest to buy - everyone agrees, the chart confirms it. But entering on a vertical move means your stop is far away, your R:R is terrible, and you are exit liquidity for earlier buyers. Great trades usually feel uncomfortable at entry, not obvious.

A trading journal - every entry, exit, size and reason - converts vague feelings into visible patterns: my Sunday-night trades all lose, I always cut winners early. It is unglamorous and it is the fastest self-improvement tool trading has. Fake-money trades count too.

quiz.q: The classic revenge trade happens…
o: After careful planning and a detailed written checklist
Minutes after a painful loss, oversized

quiz.q: Buying a coin that is already up 30% today usually means…
The main purpose of a trading journal is…
o: Making your patterns visible so you can fix them
Predicting where the market is likely to go next

try.p: Your paper trades already feed a free analytics journal - see your win rate, streaks and habits.
try.label: Trading Journal →

lessons.t: The daily loss limit and tilt

cards.p: After two or three losses, your brain chemistry changes - the need to win it back overrides the plan. Poker players call it tilt, and they manage it structurally, not with willpower: when a limit is hit, the session ends. No exceptions, no one more trade.

Decide in advance: lose X% of the account in a day (commonly 2-3R) and you are done until tomorrow. The market reopens every day; your discipline does not regenerate mid-tilt. The best trade you will make on a bad day is closing the laptop.

A rule you must remember while tilted will fail. Write the limit in your journal, tell someone, set an alarm - anything that makes stopping the default instead of a choice. Consistency here is worth more than any indicator you will ever learn.

quiz.q: Tilt is…
o: A chart pattern that appears at the top of a rally
The compromised state after losses where revenge overrides the plan

quiz.q: A daily loss limit works because…
o: It predicts when the market is about to turn against you
It ends the session BEFORE tilt does maximum damage

quiz.q: The best defence against tilt is…
o: Strong willpower summoned in the heat of the moment
A mechanical, pre-decided stop to the session

cards.p: Long BTC, long ETH and long SOL feels diversified. It is not: in stress, crypto correlations go to nearly 1 - everything falls together. You are not holding three trades; you are holding one trade at triple size, with triple the liquidation surface.

cards.h: Real diversification in crypto is rare
cards.p: Within crypto, almost everything is a leveraged bet on the same tide (Bitcoin and global liquidity). Some pairs decorrelate in calm times - and recorrelate exactly when it hurts. Assume correlation = 1 in your risk math and you will never be surprised.

Your risk per trade rule must apply to the SUM of correlated positions. Three 1%-risk longs on majors is a 3% bet on one outcome. Either size each smaller, or accept and name the concentration - but never call it diversification.

quiz.q: Long BTC + long ETH + long SOL in a crash behaves like…
In market stress, crypto correlations typically…
o: Fall to zero as every coin moves independently
Go to nearly 1 - everything moves together

quiz.q: Your 1% risk rule should apply to…

try.p: See how tightly the majors actually move together - the live correlation matrix makes it visceral.
try.label: Correlation Matrix →

lessons.t: A+ setups: the skill of skipping

cards.h: Your edge lives in a few trades
cards.p: Review any profitable journal and a pattern appears: most of the profit came from a minority of high-quality setups, and most of the losses from filler - boredom trades, almost-setups, revenge entries. The fastest performance upgrade is deleting the filler.

cards.h: Define A+ before you see the chart
cards.p: Write down what your best setup looks like: trend aligned, key level, confluence, clean invalidation, R:R at least 2. If a trade does not tick the list, it does not exist. Vague standards get negotiated away in real time; written ones survive.

The market punishes the need for action. Flat is a position - often the best one. Professionals describe their job as waiting; amateurs describe it as trading. The difference shows up directly in the expectancy math you learned in r3.

quiz.q: In most profitable journals, the bulk of profit comes from…
o: Every trade contributing an equal share of profit

quiz.q: An A+ setup should be defined…
o: While staring at a live chart
In writing, before you see the chart

quiz.q: Being flat (no position) is…
o: Wasted time that a serious trader cannot afford
A position - often the best one

cards.h: Entries do not have to be all-or-nothing
cards.p: Scaling in means building a position in parts - a third at market, a third at a better level, a third on confirmation. You trade some average-price precision for flexibility, and no single fill decides the trade.

Scaling into a WINNING thesis at planned levels is a strategy. Doubling into a LOSING trade to lower your average - martingale - is how accounts die: your size is largest exactly when you are most wrong. The difference is whether the adds were planned before entry.

Selling a winner in parts (r10 covered the first slice) smooths the exit the same way. The rule that keeps all of this honest: every add and every trim was written in the plan BEFORE the position existed. Improvised adds are tilt wearing a strategy costume.

quiz.q: The difference between scaling in and martingale is…
o: Whether the adds were planned before entry vs doubling a losing trade
Nothing - they are two names for the same thing

quiz.q: Martingale sizing means your biggest size arrives…
o: At the moment when you are most right about the market
Exactly when you are most wrong

quiz.q: Improvised mid-trade adds are usually…
o: A sign of genius reading of the market in real time

lessons.t: Risk of ruin: the math of survival

cards.h: Ruin is a probability you can compute
cards.p: Given a win rate, an R:R and a risk-per-trade, the chance your account ever hits a fatal drawdown is computable - it is called risk of ruin. The brutal insight: at high per-trade risk, even a genuinely profitable strategy carries a HIGH chance of ruin before the edge pays.

A 50%-win-rate, 1:2 strategy at 2% risk has near-zero ruin probability. The identical strategy at 15% risk will, with high probability, hit a killing streak eventually. The strategy did not change - only the bet size did. Survival is a sizing property, not a skill property.

Do not take this on faith: put your paper-trading win rate and R:R into a risk-of-ruin calculator and move the risk slider. Watching your own survival odds collapse as risk grows past 5% teaches sizing better than any paragraph.

quiz.q: Risk of ruin depends on…
o: Win rate, R:R and risk per trade
Only the specific coin you choose to trade

quiz.q: A profitable strategy at 15% risk per trade…
o: Still carries a high chance of ruin from a normal streak
Has no meaningful drawdowns along the way

quiz.q: Survival is primarily a property of…

try.p: Feed your real win rate and R:R into the calculator and drag the risk slider - watch your ruin odds move.
try.label: Risk of Ruin Calculator →

cards.h: Pilots do not trust memory. Neither should you.
cards.p: Under stress, humans skip steps - that is why aviation runs on checklists. A pre-trade checklist externalises your discipline: five questions answered in writing before any entry, every time, especially when the setup feels urgent.

1) Is the trade WITH the higher-timeframe trend? 2) Is it at a level, with confluence? 3) Where exactly is the invalidation (stop), and is R:R at least 2? 4) Is the size correct for 1-2% risk? 5) Is there a scheduled event (CPI, FOMC) inside the trade window?

cards.h: Urgency is the enemy of the list
cards.p: The trades that most need the checklist are the ones that feel too urgent for it - the vertical breakout, the revenge setup. If a trade cannot wait sixty seconds for five questions, it is not a trade; it is an impulse with a chart attached.

quiz.q: Checklists exist because…
o: Under stress humans reliably skip steps
They help predict where price will go next

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the five checks?
A trade that cannot wait 60 seconds for the checklist is…
o: The best kind - real opportunities never wait
An impulse with a chart attached

lessons.t: Review your journal like a coach

cards.p: Once a week, read every trade like a coach reviewing game tape: was the entry per plan? Was the exit? Which rule was broken, and what did breaking it cost? The goal is not self-flagellation - it is finding the ONE repeated leak that costs the most.

Group your trades: by setup type, by day of week, by session, by coin, by emotional state if you log it. Leaks hide in aggregates and jump out of slices - Sunday-night trades losing, one setup carrying everything, longs outperforming shorts 3 to 1.

Do not fix everything at once. Pick the single most expensive pattern, write one rule against it, and check next week whether it held. Compounding tiny process improvements is exactly like compounding capital - slow, boring and unreasonably powerful.

quiz.q: The purpose of a weekly review is…
o: Finding the single most expensive repeated leak
Counting the week's profits and celebrating the wins

quiz.q: Leaks are easiest to find by…
The best improvement cadence is…
o: Fixing everything at once in a single big overhaul
One leak, one rule, one week at a time

cards.h: Trade with the current, not against it
cards.p: A trend is a sequence of higher highs and higher lows (up) or lower highs and lower lows (down). Trading against a strong trend because something looks too high or too cheap is a donation. The trend is not always right - but it is right more often than your feelings about it.

act.prompt: Buyers stepped in at the same area three times. Tap that zone.

cards.p: Support and resistance are zones, not exact lines. Train your eye on this chart.

One level means little. A level that coincides with a trend line, a round number and a prior high is confluence - several independent reasons pointing at the same zone. Professionals wait for confluence; beginners act on the first line they draw.

quiz.q: An uptrend is defined by…
o: A long series of green candles, whatever the structure

quiz.q: When resistance breaks, it often…
Confluence means…
o: Several independent signals pointing at the same zone
Trading several different coins at the same time

try.p: Draw your first levels: open a chart, mark the most recent obvious support and resistance zones.
try.label: Open Charts →

cards.p: A moving average draws the average closing price of the last N candles - the market's recent memory as one smooth line. Price above a rising MA is trend-healthy; price chopping through a flat MA means no trend exists and trend tools will just generate noise.

cards.h: EMA vs SMA, and the famous pairs
cards.p: The simple MA (SMA) weights every candle equally; the exponential MA (EMA) reacts faster to recent prices. Watched-by-everyone settings: EMA 9/21 for short-term momentum, SMA 50/200 for the big picture. They work partly BECAUSE everyone watches them - self-fulfilling zones.

When the 50 crosses above the 200 (golden cross), it confirms an uptrend is established; the reverse (death cross) confirms a downtrend. Note the word confirms - MAs are lagging by construction. They tell you which side to trade FROM, not the exact moment to click.

quiz.q: A moving average shows…
o: The price the market expects in the near future
The average of recent closes - the trend smoothed

quiz.q: Which MA reacts faster to fresh price moves?
A golden cross (50 over 200) is best used as…
o: A precise timer for the exact entry moment

cards.p: RSI compresses the last 14 candles of gains vs losses into a 0-100 scale. Above 70 the market is called overbought, below 30 oversold. It measures the SPEED of the move, not its correctness - a market can be overbought and keep rising for weeks.

Selling just because RSI touched 70 is one of the most reliable ways to short a raging bull trend. In strong trends, RSI stays pinned in extreme territory. The overbought/oversold reading only becomes interesting when the trend is ALREADY weakening or at major levels.

When price makes a new high but RSI makes a lower high, momentum is fading under the surface - that is bearish divergence, an early caution flag (not a sell button). The reverse at lows is bullish divergence. Divergence plus a key level plus confluence - now it is a setup.

quiz.q: RSI above 70 means…
o: A guaranteed reversal, so experienced traders sell into it immediately
The recent move has been fast; in strong trends it can stay there

quiz.q: Bearish divergence is…
On its own, a single indicator reading is…
o: A complete strategy on its own for most traders
Weak - it needs confluence with levels and trend

cards.h: Open interest: money in the game
cards.p: Open interest (OI) counts the total value of futures positions currently open. Rising OI with rising price = new money buying the move (healthy). Rising price with FALLING OI = shorts closing, not new demand - a move likely to stall. OI tells you WHO is powering a move.

The long/short ratio shows which side the crowd is on. Extreme readings are contrarian: when nearly everyone is already long, few buyers remain - but a huge pool of liquidation prices sits below, ready to fuel the opposite move.

The high-conviction derivative setup stacks three things: one-sided long/short ratio + rising OI + funding paying the crowded side. That is a crowd that is leveraged, growing, and paying to stay - a loaded spring. Any one signal alone is weak; together they are the market's tell.

quiz.q: Price rising while open interest falls usually means…
An extremely one-sided long/short ratio is…
o: A signal to join the majority

quiz.q: The loaded spring setup combines…
o: RSI, MACD and volume all pointing the same way
Crowded ratio + rising OI + funding paying that side

try.p: Check the live long/short ratio and open interest - which side is crowded right now?
try.label: Long/Short Ratio →

cards.p: When price hits a leveraged trader's liquidation level, the exchange force-sells the position at market. That sell pushes price down - into the NEXT cluster of liquidation prices, triggering more forced sells. Watch the dominoes below: one trigger, a chain of forced exits.

Liquidation prices cluster at predictable places - just beyond round numbers and obvious support, where crowds of similar traders opened similar positions. Large players can see these clusters. A wick that spikes through a level, triggers the cluster and instantly reverses is that mechanism working.

Live liquidation feeds show cascades as they happen - a burst of forced longs marks capitulation lows more reliably than most indicators. For your own trades the lesson is defensive: put your liquidation price where a routine hunt cannot reach it, or better, size so liquidation is impossible.

quiz.q: A liquidation cascade is…
o: A planned exchange event announced well in advance
Forced sells triggering more forced sells in a chain

quiz.q: Liquidation clusters form…
o: Randomly across the whole chart with no pattern at all
Just beyond round numbers and obvious support levels

quiz.q: The defensive lesson for your own trades is…
o: Use the maximum leverage the exchange will allow you
Keep your liquidation out of routine wick range

try.p: Watch forced liquidations stream in live on Rekt - see the cascade mechanism with your own eyes.
try.label: Open Rekt →

lessons.t: Macro: the tide under every trade

cards.h: Crypto trades the dollar and rates
cards.p: Bitcoin is a liquidity-sensitive risk asset: when rates look set to fall, money flows toward risk and crypto rises; higher-for-longer does the opposite. This is why a US inflation number can move Bitcoin within one second - algorithms reprice the entire rate path instantly.

A handful of scheduled releases drive the biggest hours in crypto: the Fed's FOMC rate decision, CPI and PCE inflation prints, and the NFP jobs report. They are on the calendar weeks ahead - being surprised by one is a choice. Below: what 12:30 UTC on CPI day looks like.

cards.h: Event risk is a sizing problem
cards.p: You cannot predict the number, but you can survive it: know the release time, and size so a 2-3% instant wick cannot liquidate you. The first candle after a release is frequently a fake-out - professionals let it play out rather than market-chasing at the worst spread of the day.

quiz.q: Why does a US inflation print move Bitcoin in seconds?
o: Miners dump their holdings the moment news is published

quiz.q: FOMC, CPI and NFP release times are…
o: Scheduled and public weeks in advance
Relevant only for stock traders, not for crypto

quiz.q: The professional approach to a big scheduled release is…
o: Max out your leverage right before the number drops
Size so an instant 2-3% wick cannot liquidate you

quiz.q: The single most important idea in this course so far was…
o: Finding perfect entries on the smallest timeframes

try.p: Open the economic calendar and find the next FOMC or CPI date - set a reminder before it hits.
try.label: Economic Calendar →

cards.p: Triangles, flags, ranges - under every named pattern is one physical fact: volatility COMPRESSES as buyers and sellers reach temporary agreement, then EXPANDS when one side wins. The name matters less than recognising compression, because expansion follows it.

A triangle does not know which way it will break. Patterns tilt odds slightly and - more usefully - give you clean invalidation levels: enter on the break, stop beyond the opposite side. The R:R structure is the real gift, not prediction.

Stare long enough and any chart grows patterns like clouds grow faces. Anchor patterns to the context you already have - trend, key levels, volume on the break. A textbook flag against the higher-timeframe trend at no level is just a shape.

quiz.q: Underneath every chart pattern is…
o: Insider trading by well-connected large players

quiz.q: The most useful thing a pattern gives you is…
o: A guaranteed direction for the coming breakout
A clean invalidation level for R:R structure

quiz.q: A perfect flag against the higher-timeframe trend at no level is…
o: An A+ setup worth full size and full conviction

cards.p: The daily chart sets the WEATHER (trend and key levels), the 4-hour sets the SETUP (structure forming at those levels), the 15-minute sets the TRIGGER (precise entry and stop). One market, three altitudes - confusion happens when you trade a trigger without weather.

Always in this order: daily first (which side am I allowed to trade?), then 4H (is a setup forming at a level that matters?), then LTF (exact entry, exact invalidation). Reversing the order - finding an exciting 5-minute chart and inventing a story - is how counter-trend donations happen.

When timeframes disagree, the higher one wins. A bullish 15-minute inside a bearish daily is a bounce to sell, not a reversal to marry. Structure breaks propagate upward slowly - respect the big map until it actually changes.

quiz.q: The correct analysis order is…
When timeframes conflict, priority goes to…
A bullish 15m inside a bearish daily is usually…

cards.p: Bitcoin dominance (BTC.D) is Bitcoin's share of total crypto market cap. Rising dominance: money favours BTC - alts bleed even in green markets. Falling dominance with rising prices: risk appetite is spilling outward - the classic alt-season signature.

Liquidity typically cascades: into BTC first, then ETH, then large caps, then the long tail of small alts - each wave riskier than the last. By the time micro-caps go vertical, the cycle is late. Dominance charts let you see which chapter you are in.

cards.h: Trading the tide, not just the boat
cards.p: An altcoin long is really two bets: the coin AND the dominance tide. A strong alt setup against rising BTC.D is swimming upstream. Check the tide before the trade - it is one extra chart and it reframes everything.

quiz.q: Rising BTC dominance means…
The classic liquidity rotation runs…
o: From the smallest caps straight into BTC
BTC → ETH → large caps → small caps

quiz.q: An altcoin long during rising dominance is…

cards.p: Since US spot Bitcoin ETFs launched in 2024, institutional demand became measurable: every inflow forces the fund to buy real BTC, every outflow forces selling - reported daily. It is the clearest window crypto has ever had into big, slow money.

A rally powered by ETF inflows has real coins being taken off the market - durable fuel. A rally with outflows and spiking funding is leverage lifting its own weight - the kind that cascades (m5). Flows tell you which rally you are standing in.

One red day of flows means little; a multi-week streak is a regime. Combine the flow trend with funding and open interest for the full picture of who is driving - the same three-signal thinking you learned in m4, now with an institutional layer.

quiz.q: An ETF inflow forces the issuer to…
o: Buy real BTC to back new shares

quiz.q: A rally with ETF outflows and spiking funding is powered by…
o: Large institutions accumulating for the long term

quiz.q: Flows matter most as…
o: Single-day ticks that reveal each day's winner
Multi-week trends alongside funding and OI

cards.p: Sentiment gauges like the Fear & Greed index compress volatility, momentum, social buzz and dominance into one number. It is a thermometer for emotion - useful precisely because crowds are most wrong at their emotional extremes.

cards.h: Extremes are signals, the middle is noise
cards.p: A reading of 55 tells you nothing. Extreme greed says late-comers are piling in with leverage - check funding and the long/short ratio for confirmation. Extreme fear marks the capitulation zones where forced sellers finish and patient buyers begin.

cards.h: Use it as a brake, not an engine
cards.p: Sentiment does not generate entries; it moderates size and aggression. In extreme greed, tighten risk on longs even if the chart still looks perfect. In extreme fear, resist panic-selling into the hole. It is a discipline tool wearing a data costume.

quiz.q: Sentiment indexes are most useful at…
o: Neutral readings in the middle of the scale
Emotional extremes, where crowds are most wrong

quiz.q: Extreme greed combined with high funding suggests…
o: A safe entry backed by broad market agreement
Late leveraged longs - elevated squeeze risk

quiz.q: Sentiment works best as…
o: A brake on size and aggression

try.p: Check where the market's emotions sit right now - live Fear & Greed with history.
try.label: Fear & Greed Index →

cards.p: A thesis stacks everything this course taught into one paragraph: higher-timeframe trend and level (m1, m8), pattern or structure (m7), derivative positioning - funding, OI, long/short (m4, l5), the macro calendar (m6), and flows or sentiment as the regime layer (m10, m11).

The second half is Course 3: exact invalidation, R:R of at least 2, size from the 1-2% rule, planned partials, and the event check. A thesis without the risk half is a market opinion - opinions are free and cost the most.

cards.h: Write it, trade it, grade it
cards.p: Write the thesis BEFORE entry, execute it as written, then grade the PROCESS in your journal - not the outcome. A perfectly executed loss is a good trade; a lucky, plan-breaking win is a bad one that will bill you later. This loop, repeated, is the entire craft.

quiz.q: A complete thesis includes…
o: Trend, level, positioning data, macro AND the full risk plan
A consensus of respected voices on social media

o: Efficient - less time wasted on paperwork
Just an opinion - the expensive kind

quiz.q: You should grade your trades on…
o: The outcome only - profit is what counts

quiz.q: Across this whole course, the single most important idea is…

courses.name: Advanced Market Structure
courses.sub: Where orders live and why price goes there

lessons.t: Liquidity: where the orders actually live

cards.p: Big players cannot fill large positions where the book is empty - they need resting orders to trade against. Clusters of stop-losses and liquidations ARE those resting orders. That is why price so often spikes through an obvious level, fills there, and reverses: it went shopping.

Your stop-loss below support is a sell order waiting to happen. A thousand traders placing it in the same obvious spot creates a pool of guaranteed sellers - the perfect place for a large buyer to absorb. This is not a conspiracy; it is simply how large size gets filled.

You cannot avoid the game, but you can stop being the easiest target: place invalidations beyond the obvious pools, expect the sweep-and-reverse at clean levels, and treat a wick through a level that instantly reclaims it as information - someone just got filled.

quiz.q: Why does price often spike through obvious levels and reverse?
o: Pure random chance in an unpredictable market
Large players fill against the stops clustered there

quiz.q: A cluster of stop-losses below support is effectively…
o: Protection that big players cannot touch
A pool of guaranteed sell orders

quiz.q: A wick through a level that instantly reclaims it suggests…

cards.h: Sideways is where the story is written
cards.p: Trends are the result; ranges are the cause. In a range, large players quietly build (accumulate) or unload (distribute) positions without moving price against themselves. The breakout direction is usually decided long before it happens - inside the range.

Watch how price behaves at the range edges: repeated probes below the low that recover fast (sweeps into demand) hint at accumulation; failing rallies at the high on shrinking volume hint at distribution. The middle of the range is noise - the edges are the tell.

The classic ending: a false breakout AGAINST the real direction - the spring - that sweeps stops, fills the big player's final size, and reverses into the true move. If you learn to expect the trap, the trap becomes your entry instead of your exit.

quiz.q: Large positions are typically built…
The most informative part of a range is…
A spring is…
o: A false breakout against the real direction
A moving average crossing back over price

lessons.t: Imbalances: when price moves too fast

cards.p: When price moves violently in one direction, it skips levels - barely any trading happened there. That thin zone is an imbalance (often called a fair value gap). Markets frequently revisit these zones later, because untraded prices are unfinished business for the auction.

Nothing mystical: participants who missed the move leave orders in the skipped zone, and market makers who sold into the spike look to buy back where volume was thin. The zone acts like a magnet not because of magic, but because orders accumulate there.

An imbalance is a CANDIDATE zone for entries in the trend direction - never a guarantee. Stack it with structure: an imbalance that overlaps a support level and the higher-timeframe trend is a real setup; a lone gap on a 1-minute chart is noise with a fancy name.

quiz.q: An imbalance (fair value gap) is…
o: A broken chart caused by missing exchange data
A zone price skipped with barely any trading

quiz.q: Price often revisits imbalances because…
o: Missed orders accumulate in the thin zone
Regulators require gaps to be filled quickly

quiz.q: An imbalance becomes a real setup when…
o: It overlaps structure and the higher-timeframe trend
It prints clearly on the 1-minute chart during quiet hours

cards.h: Volume by PRICE, not by time
cards.p: The volume bars under your chart show volume per time period. A volume profile turns them sideways: how much traded at each PRICE. High-volume nodes are prices the market accepted for a long time; low-volume nodes are prices it rejected quickly.

Price entering a high-volume node tends to slow down and chop - plenty of business was done there, and it attracts trade again. Price entering a low-volume node tends to slice through fast - nobody wanted to trade there before, and nobody does now. This explains many fast moves better than any indicator.

Mark the highest-volume node of the recent range (the point of control). Above it, dips into it often find buyers; below it, rallies into it often find sellers. Combine with your levels from m1 - when a volume node and a structural level agree, you have found a real zone.

quiz.q: A volume profile shows volume…
o: Per hour of the trading day

quiz.q: Price moving through a LOW-volume node usually…
The point of control is…
o: The price with the highest traded volume
A candle pattern found at the range edges

cards.p: Fibonacci retracements mark fixed fractions of a prior move - 38.2%, 50%, 61.8%. There is no physical law forcing price to respect them. And yet they often do get respected. Why? Because millions of traders draw the same levels and act on them - a self-fulfilling mirror.

cards.h: The honest way to use them
cards.p: Treat fibs as a MAP of where other traders expect reactions, not as gravity. The 61.8% retracement in an uptrend is a popular buy zone - which makes it a real zone, whatever you believe about the math. Self-fulfilling is still fulfilling.

A fib level alone is a coin flip dressed in mathematics. A fib level that lands on a volume node, a prior support and the higher-timeframe trendline is a zone with several independent reasons to matter. By now you know the pattern: nothing works alone; stacks work.

quiz.q: Fibonacci levels often work because…
o: Enough traders watch and act on the same levels
Exchanges enforce them in their matching engines

quiz.q: The honest use of a fib retracement is…
o: A map of where crowds expect reactions

quiz.q: A fib level with no other confluence is…
o: An A+ setup ready for full position size
Roughly a coin flip in fancy clothes

lessons.t: Relative strength: pick the strongest horse

cards.p: When the market bounces, some coins recover to new highs while others barely lift off their lows. That difference - relative strength - is one of the most durable edges in trading: what refused to fall in the storm usually leads the recovery.

No indicator needed: when BTC dipped 5%, what did your candidate do? The coin that fell 2% has buyers defending it; the one that fell 12% does not. Compare a handful of charts against BTC over the same window and the leaders reveal themselves.

Combine with m9: in a risk-on tape with falling dominance, longing the relatively strongest alts is fishing where the fish are - trend, tide and strength aligned. Longing the weakest coin because it is cheap is the exact opposite trade wearing a discount sticker.

quiz.q: Relative strength compares…
o: A coin's current price against its own history alone
How a coin performs versus the market

quiz.q: In a market dip, the coin that fell least likely has…
o: Buyers defending it - strength worth noting
Low liquidity and nothing more than that

quiz.q: Buying the WEAKEST coin because it looks cheap is…
o: The professional move most beginners miss

cards.p: Markets alternate between regimes: long stretches of tight, quiet ranges and bursts of violent expansion. Volatility clusters - calm follows calm, storm follows storm - until the regime breaks. The same strategy cannot treat both worlds identically.

In a storm regime, a stop that was sensible last week now sits inside the noise - and your size must shrink to keep risk constant (bigger stop distance × smaller size = same 1% risk). In dead-calm regimes, breakout trades die repeatedly while mean-reversion thrives.

Add one question to your checklist: what regime am I in? A glance at recent candle sizes or an ATR reading answers it. Most inexplicable losing streaks are a strategy built for one regime being run in the other.

quiz.q: Volatility tends to…
o: Be completely random from one day to the next
Cluster - calm follows calm, storm follows storm

quiz.q: In a high-volatility regime, keeping risk constant means…
Many losing streaks are really…
o: A strategy built for one regime running in the other
Manipulation by market makers hunting retail

cards.p: You now hold many lenses: structure, liquidity, ranges, imbalances, volume nodes, fibs, relative strength, regimes - plus everything from courses 1-4. A professional does not use all of them everywhere; they define a fixed STACK that must align before a trade exists.

Example stack: higher-timeframe trend + a structural level + a volume node agreeing + positioning not crowded against you + no red-calendar event inside the window. Five checks. Your stack can differ - what matters is that it is WRITTEN and fixed, so every trade is comparable in the journal.

A real stack filters brutally: most days produce nothing, and that is the design. The trades that pass carry several independent reasons - which is exactly what makes their R:R honest. This is the bridge from knowing things to having an edge.

quiz.q: A confluence system is…
o: Using every available indicator at the same time
A fixed, written stack of conditions that must align

quiz.q: A proper stack produces…
o: A constant stream of trades every single day
Few trades, each with several independent reasons

quiz.q: The stack must be written down so that…
o: It looks professional when shown to other traders
Every trade is comparable and reviewable in the journal

try.p: Open the charts workspace and mark ONE complete stack on any coin: trend, level, volume node, and check positioning. No trade needed - just the read.

cards.p: Every discretionary decision is a chance for tilt, FOMO and hindsight to leak in. A system - fixed rules for setup, entry, exit and size - removes the decision at the moment of maximum emotion. Most traders do not need better instincts; they need fewer opportunities to use them.

If your entries are moods, your journal reviews are astrology. If your entries are rules, every trade is a data point: THIS setup, taken THIS way, produces THIS expectancy. Only rule-based trading can actually be improved, because only it can be measured.

cards.h: Discretion has a place - at the design desk
cards.p: The skill does not disappear; it moves. You use judgement to DESIGN and REVIEW the rules - weekly, calmly, away from live prices. The machine (or the checklist) executes. Judgement at the desk, discipline at the trigger.

quiz.q: The main advantage of a rules-based system is…
o: Guaranteed profit once the rules are finished
Removing decisions at the moment of maximum emotion

quiz.q: Mood-based entries make your journal…
o: More fun to read back at the end of the week
Unmeasurable - you cannot improve what you cannot compare

quiz.q: In systematic trading, human judgement belongs…

cards.p: Before risking a cent - or even paper time - you can ask history: had I traded these exact rules for the last year, what would have happened? That is a backtest. It will not promise the future, but it executes rules with zero hindsight and zero mercy.

cards.h: What a backtest actually tells you
cards.p: Not \u201cthis will make money\u201d - rather: the strategy's PROFILE. Win rate, average R, worst losing streak, deepest drawdown, how many trades per month. You already know from r10 that these numbers, with sizing, decide survival. The backtest hands them to you in minutes.

Backtests assume fills at historical prices - real spread, slippage and funding will be worse. Treat backtest results as the OPTIMISTIC ceiling, subtract costs mentally, and only trust profiles that survive that haircut with room to spare.

quiz.q: A backtest tells you…
o: The historical profile of your exact rules
Which coin is going to pump next week

quiz.q: Backtest results versus live results are usually…
o: Optimistic - real costs make live worse

quiz.q: The right way to read a backtest is…
o: As an optimistic ceiling minus costs
As entertainment for the weekend, nothing more
