try.label: Strategy Backtester →

cards.h: The perfect backtest that never works
cards.p: Tune a strategy's parameters long enough and it will fit the past PERFECTLY - because it has memorised the noise, not learned the signal. That is overfitting: the more beautiful the backtest curve after heavy tuning, the more suspicious you should be.

Warning signs: many finely-tuned parameters (why 13.5 and not 14?), performance that collapses when you shift the test window by a month, an edge that only exists on one coin and one timeframe. Robust edges are usually simple, slightly ugly, and work broadly.

Every parameter you add is another way to memorise the past. Prefer strategies with 2-3 knobs over 10. If small parameter changes cause big result changes, you have fit noise. A mediocre backtest that is STABLE beats a spectacular one that is fragile.

quiz.q: Overfitting means…
o: Trading far too much in a single session
Tuning rules until they memorise past noise

quiz.q: A suspicious sign of overfitting is…
o: Performance collapsing when the window shifts
Working consistently across many different coins

quiz.q: Between a stable mediocre backtest and a fragile spectacular one, choose…

cards.h: Never grade on the training data
cards.p: The fix for overfitting is discipline in testing: design and tune your rules on ONE slice of history (in-sample), then run them UNTOUCHED on a slice they have never seen (out-of-sample). Only the out-of-sample result counts - it is the closest thing to the future you can buy.

Walk-forward testing repeats this on a rolling window: tune on months 1-6, test on month 7; slide forward; repeat. A strategy that keeps performing on data it never saw has earned some trust. One that only shines in-sample has earned none.

cards.h: Paper trading is the final out-of-sample
cards.p: After the tests, run the system on live prices with fake money - the one dataset that cannot be peeked at: the present. If backtest, out-of-sample AND paper agree, you have something. If they disagree, believe the most live one.

quiz.q: Out-of-sample testing means…
o: Testing on the data you tuned on
Testing on data the rules have never seen

quiz.q: Which result deserves the most trust?
o: The prettiest chart with the smoothest curve

quiz.q: Paper trading serves as…
o: A waste of time once the backtest is done

cards.p: You do not jump from clicking buttons to full autopilot. The ladder: written checklist → alerts that ping you when conditions align → semi-automation (the machine proposes, you confirm) → full bot. Each rung removes one human failure mode; climb only as your rules prove stable.

cards.h: What a bot needs from you
cards.p: A bot is your rules, frozen. It needs UNAMBIGUOUS conditions (no \u201clooks strong\u201d), exact position sizing, exact exits, and instructions for the ugly cases: partial fills, disconnects, gaps. Writing these down often reveals that your \u201csystem\u201d had human glue holding it together.

cards.h: Test the machine like a strategy
cards.p: A bot can lose money two ways: bad rules or bad code. Test them separately - rules in the backtester, code against a paper-trading API where a bug costs nothing. Only after both survive do real funds enter the picture, small first.

quiz.q: The sensible automation ladder starts with…
o: A full bot on day one

quiz.q: A bot requires rules that are…
o: Unambiguous, with sizing and exits defined
Flexible enough to adapt in the moment

quiz.q: A trading bot should first run against…
o: A paper-trading API where bugs cost nothing
A trusted friend's account with real funds

cards.p: A running system needs a dashboard and a leash: daily checks that fills match intentions, that risk per trade is what you set, that the market regime still resembles the one it was built for. Silent drift - in costs, in volatility, in your own rule-following - kills slowly.

Before deploying, write the kill criteria: a maximum drawdown (say 15%), a losing streak beyond backtest-worst, or a regime break. Hit any of them and the system STOPS - no renegotiation with hope. You learned this personally in r6; machines deserve the same discipline.

Exchanges go down, APIs time out, a fat-finger config doubles your size. Assume incidents, so they surprise you only mildly: position caps at the exchange level, alerts on every fill, and a manual master OFF you can hit from your phone. Boring engineering is what safety looks like.

quiz.q: Kill criteria should be defined…
A running system needs…
o: No attention at all once it is deployed
Daily checks that behaviour matches intention

quiz.q: Sound protection against incidents includes…
o: Position caps, alerts and a manual OFF
Ignoring them until they actually happen

cards.p: No single system works forever - trends end, volatility regimes flip, crowds adapt. Professionals run a small PORTFOLIO of uncorrelated systems: a trend-follower, a mean-reverter, perhaps a funding harvester. When one sleeps, another usually eats.

The hardest skill: shutting down a strategy you love. The criteria are the same kill rules from s6, plus one more - if the structural reason it worked has disappeared (a fee change, a regime shift, everyone doing it), retire it while it still has dignity. Track record is history, not entitlement.

Look at the arc: mechanics (courses 1-2), survival (3), reading the tape (4-5)… and now process that runs without your moods. Whether you automate or stay manual, the destination is the same: a written, measured, reviewed edge - and a trader calm enough to follow it.

quiz.q: Professionals run multiple systems because…
A system should be retired when…
o: The very first time it has a single red week
Kill rules hit or its structural reason disappeared

quiz.q: The end state of this whole course is…
o: A written, measured, reviewed edge followed calmly
A secret indicator nobody else has discovered

courses.name: Going Live
courses.sub: From paper to real, without dying

lessons.t: Are you ready? The honest metrics

cards.p: Going live is not a feeling - it is a checklist: at least 100 paper trades, positive expectancy across 3 consecutive months, a journal you actually keep, a written strategy with defined A+ setups, and zero revenge-trading incidents in the last month.

Assume your live performance will be WORSE than paper at first - execution hesitation, emotional interference, spread and fees you barely noticed. If your paper edge is thin, real conditions will erase it. You want a margin of safety in the numbers, not a coin flip.

Nobody hands out medals for going live early, and the market will still be here next year. Every month of disciplined paper trading is cheap tuition; every premature live month is expensive tuition for the same lesson. The patient path and the fast path end at the same place - one just costs more.

quiz.q: A reasonable readiness bar includes…
o: 100+ trades and 3 months of positive expectancy
A hot streak running through the current week

quiz.q: Your first live months will likely perform…
Going live early earns you…
o: Better fees from the exchange loyalty tiers

cards.p: 1) Is it legal and available in YOUR country - regulation decides everything downstream. 2) Is it liquid in the pairs you trade - thin books eat profits. 3) What are the REAL fees at your size, including funding. 4) What is its security and solvency history - has it ever frozen withdrawals?

An exchange account is a trading venue, not a savings account. Keep only active trading capital there; withdraw profits on a schedule. Enable every security feature - authenticator 2FA, withdrawal allow-lists, anti-phishing codes - before the first deposit, not after the first scare.

A regulated venue in your jurisdiction with modest leverage beats an offshore casino with a 100x button - you now know the 100x button is not the prize, survival is. Deposit small, verify the full loop (deposit → trade → withdraw) with a trivial amount first.

quiz.q: The FIRST question when choosing an exchange is…
o: Is it legal and available in your country
The size of the sign-up bonuses on offer

quiz.q: How much should live on an exchange account?
o: Everything, so it can compound faster

quiz.q: Before real size, you should first…
o: Test the full loop with a trivial amount
Disable 2FA temporarily to speed things up

cards.p: Your first live trades should risk about a TENTH of your normal paper risk - small enough that the outcome is irrelevant. The goal is not profit; it is executing your full process (checklist, entry, stop, journal) while real feelings fire for the first time.

Success in week one is: trades that look exactly like your paper trades, just smaller. Same setups, same sizing math, same exits. If your live trading immediately looks different from your paper trading - more trades, bigger size, no stops - stop and go back to paper.

cards.h: Scale by calendar, not by confidence
cards.p: Increase size on a schedule (for example, monthly) and only if the month was disciplined - never mid-week because you feel hot. Feelings of invincibility are a lagging indicator of a winning streak and a leading indicator of the give-back.

quiz.q: First live trades should risk…
Success in your first live week looks like…
o: Trades identical to your paper trades
Constant action across many different pairs

quiz.q: Size should increase…
o: Whenever you feel hot and confident enough
On a schedule, after disciplined months

cards.p: Paper losses are information; real losses are pain. Expect to cut winners earlier, hesitate on entries and widen mental stops - everyone does at first. This is not a character flaw; it is your brain treating money as survival. Naming it is half the fix.

The professional heuristic: if a position affects your sleep, your mood or your relationships, it is too big - regardless of what the risk math allows. Trade a size where you can follow the plan with total indifference to any single outcome. Indifference is the edge.

Under real pressure, your process is what you practised, not what you know. This is why the paper months mattered: checklist, journal, loss limits - drilled until they run on autopilot. When emotions spike, the autopilot flies the plane.

quiz.q: Cutting winners early when going live is…
o: A near-universal first reaction to real money
A deliberate strategy used by professionals

quiz.q: If a position affects your sleep, it is…
o: Too big, regardless of the math
A healthy sign of real commitment to the craft

quiz.q: Under pressure, you perform…
o: Better than usual thanks to adrenaline

cards.p: Every lesson in this academy reduces to one sentence: stay in the game. Edges are found, lost and refound; markets change regimes; strategies decay. The trader still standing - capital intact, process intact, curiosity intact - gets every future opportunity for free.

The learning loop never ends: trade the plan, journal everything, review weekly, kill one leak, repeat. Add tools as they earn their place - the calendar for events, funding and OI for positioning, the screener for candidates. Complexity is earned, never bolted on.

cards.h: You now know more than most
cards.p: Leverage math, liquidation mechanics, sizing, R:R, expectancy, tilt control, market structure, positioning data, macro events - this is genuinely more than the majority of people who fund a futures account ever learn. Keep practising it where mistakes are free, and let the levels mark the road ahead.

quiz.q: The one-sentence summary of the entire academy is…
The learning loop is…
o: Finished once this final course is complete

quiz.q: Complexity in a trading process should be…
o: Added immediately, while motivation is high
Earned - each tool must prove its place
